sm: The author argues that plagiarism is not itself a sin, but a broad category of conduct that can involve sins such as lying or stealing. He says the people most upset by his claim are often professionally involved in Christian writing, publishing, and theology. In his view, evangelical intellectuals have an identity problem, because their theology says the substance of their field belongs to every believer, who is also obliged to test teachers against Scripture. Academics instead rely on an economy of citations, credentials, and recognition, which he calls ideological tenure. On that reading, calling plagiarism stealing means being deprived of recognition, the currency of the profession, rather than of actual property.

The author says generative AI threatens writers whose distinction rests on polished prose, citing a 2023 study in Science that found AI helped weaker writers the most. He suggests the credentialed class may protect its status by making professional distinctions a matter of Christian obedience, though he doesn't claim everyone upset is consciously doing so. He accepts academic citation standards for term papers, but says teaching your kids or using a distinction you've internalized over decades is just learning. He points to Paul telling Timothy to entrust what he learned to faithful men, not to collect royalties. He urges giving credit where due, but says anyone accusing another Christian of sin must show the lie, the theft, or the cheating. He ends by saying the academy has its conventions but not its own Sinai, and points readers to his longer article.
